title: No Eclipse Glasses? Try a Colander!
summary: Have you ever looked through a colander? It's that bowl with holes used to drain spaghetti. Guess what? It can also help you watch a solar eclipse! On Wednesday evening, people in the UK will see a partial eclipse. That's when the Moon covers part of the Sun. It's the biggest eclipse in the UK since 1999. But you must never look directly at the Sun. It can hurt your eyes badly. Sunglasses won't help either. They don't block enough UV light. UV light is the invisible light from the Sun that can damage your eyes. So what can you do? Make a pinhole projector! Take a piece of card and poke a small hole in the middle with a pen tip. Hold the card in one hand and a blank piece of paper in the other. Turn your back to the Sun. Then line up the card and paper so the Sun's image shows on the paper. You'll see a tiny version of the eclipse! Or use a colander. Eye doctor David Jones says it's his favorite way. Hold the colander up to the Sun and look at the paper behind it. You'll see not one, but a hundred little Suns! It's like magic. So grab a colander or make a pinhole projector, and enjoy the eclipse safely!
why_it_matters: Learning how to watch an eclipse safely protects your eyes and gives you a fun science trick to try with your family.

background_read: A solar eclipse happens when the Moon moves between Earth and the Sun.
The UK (a country in Europe made up of England, Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland) does not often see a strong eclipse; the one in 1999 was a big event there.
Scientists warn that sunlight can damage your eyes even when the Sun looks dim, so special tools are needed.
Article_Structure: WHO: People in the UK who want to watch the partial eclipse.
WHAT: A partial solar eclipse can be viewed safely with a colander or a pinhole projector.
WHERE: In the UK, on Wednesday evening.
WHY: Because looking directly at the Sun can badly hurt your eyes, and sunglasses do not block enough UV light.

perspectives.description: They are happy that simple household items like a colander can make viewing safe and fun.
They warn that looking directly at the Sun is dangerous and that people need special tools, not sunglasses.
They see the eclipse as a great chance to learn about how the Sun and Moon move in space.
